config.title: Build Option helpers in TS

intro.title: Build Option helpers in TS
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a set of helper functions for working with optional values, often called 'Option' or 'Maybe' types, in TypeScript. You'll learn how to safely handle values that might be present or absent without using null or undefined directly. The core concept involves using TypeScript's generic types and union types to create a type-safe container for optional data. You'll implement functions like `some`, `none`, `map`, and `getOrElse` to transform and extract values. By the end, you'll have a reusable utility that improves code safety and expressiveness when dealing with missing data.
intro.usecase: Option helpers are essential in TypeScript applications where data might be missing or operations could fail, such as form validation systems that handle optional fields gracefully. In e-commerce checkout flows, they manage shipping address inputs that users might skip, ensuring the UI doesn't crash with undefined values. API response handlers use Option types to safely parse unpredictable data from third-party services in dashboard widgets. Search filter components rely on these helpers to build queries without null reference errors when filters are cleared.

objectives: Implement a generic Option type to represent optional values
Construct helper functions for creating Some and None variants
Apply pattern matching to safely extract values from Option types
Manipulate Option values using map and flatMap operations
Integrate Option helpers with existing TypeScript functions
Configure type guards to check for Some and None at runtime
Initialize Option values from nullable JavaScript primitives

steps.title: Import TypeScript utilities for Option helpers
steps.instruction: Create a new TypeScript file and import the 'Option' type from a hypothetical utility library. Use: import { Option } from './utils/option'
steps.hint: Start by writing an import statement at the top of your TypeScript file to bring in the Option type.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: importing a type from a module
import { User } from './models/user'
steps.expectedOutcome: The Option type is imported and ready to be used for implementing Option pattern helpers.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're importing 'Option' from the correct path: './utils/option'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. Please import Option from './utils/option' to proceed.

steps.title: Define the Option type as a union
steps.instruction: Define a generic TypeScript type called Option<T> that is a union of Some<T> and None. Use the 'type' keyword with union syntax.
steps.hint: Remember that union types in TypeScript use the pipe symbol (|) between types. The generic parameter T should be used with Some.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: a union type for API response
type ApiResponse<T> = Success<T> | Error
steps.seedCode:
import { Option } from './utils/option'

// Define the Option<T> type here
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a generic Option type that can represent either a Some containing a value of type T, or a None representing absence.
successCriteria: Option<T> is defined as a union type using type Option<T> = Some<T> | None
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using the correct union syntax with the pipe symbol and including both Some<T> and None.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Option type definition isn't quite right. Remember to use 'type' with a generic parameter T and union both Some<T> and None.

steps.title: Create the Some and None type definitions
steps.instruction: Define the Some<T> interface with a 'value' property of type T and the None type as a literal object with a discriminant property '__tag' set to 'None'.
steps.hint: Create two type definitions: an interface for Some with a generic value property, and a type alias for None as an object with a specific tag property.
steps.expectedOutcome: The code will have two new type definitions: Some<T> interface with a value property, and None type with a discriminant property.
successCriteria: Some<T> interface is defined with a 'value: T' property. None type is defined as '{ __tag: "None" }'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure Some<T> has a 'value' property of type T, and None has a discriminant property '__tag' set to 'None'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The definitions aren't quite right. Remember: Some<T> should be an interface with a 'value' property, and None should be a type with a discriminant property.

steps.title: Implement the some() helper function
steps.instruction: Create a function named 'some' that takes a value of type T and returns an object with the correct structure for the Some variant. The function should have a type parameter T and return type Some<T>.
steps.hint: Think of a function that wraps any value into the Some variant. You'll need to define a generic function that returns an object with the appropriate shape.
steps.expectedOutcome: A generic function 'some' that returns an object with the correct type structure for the Some variant.
successCriteria: The function 'some' is defined with a type parameter T, takes a parameter 'value' of type T, and returns an object with type Some<T>.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function has the correct type signature and returns an object with the proper structure.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function doesn't match the expected structure. Check the type parameter, parameter type, and return type.

steps.title: Implement the none() helper function
steps.instruction: Create a function named none that returns the None variant object with the discriminant property.
steps.hint: The function should have no parameters and return an object with a discriminant property set to 'None'.
steps.expectedOutcome: A none() function is implemented that returns the None variant object.
successCriteria: The none() function is defined and returns an object with a discriminant property set to 'None'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your none() function returns an object with the discriminant property.
steps.feedbackWrong: The none() function is not implemented correctly. It should return the None variant object.

steps.title: Create an isSome type guard
steps.instruction: Write a function named isSome that takes an Option<T> parameter and returns a type predicate 'option is Some<T>' to check if the discriminant property indicates a Some value.
steps.hint: The function should check if the option has a 'type' property equal to 'some' and return a boolean with the type predicate annotation.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a type guard function that can narrow Option<T> to Some<T> in TypeScript's type system.
successCriteria: The isSome function is defined with proper TypeScript syntax, includes a type predicate 'option is Some<T>', and checks the discriminant property correctly.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your function includes the type predicate 'option is Some<T>' and properly checks the discriminant property.
steps.feedbackWrong: The isSome function is missing or incorrect. Remember to create a function that takes Option<T> and returns a type predicate checking if the option type is 'some'.

steps.title: Create an isNone type guard
steps.instruction: Write a function named isNone that takes an Option<T> parameter and returns a type predicate 'option is None' to check if the discriminant property indicates a None value.
steps.hint: The function should check if the option has a discriminant property with value 'none'. Use the same pattern as isSome but with the opposite condition.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a complete isNone type guard function that can be used to narrow Option<T> to None in TypeScript.
successCriteria: The isNone function is defined with proper TypeScript syntax, includes the type predicate 'option is None', and correctly checks the discriminant property.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your function includes the type predicate 'option is None' and checks the discriminant property correctly.
steps.feedbackWrong: The isNone function is missing or incorrect. It should be a type guard that returns true when the option is None.

steps.title: Implement the map() helper for Option
steps.instruction: Create a function named map that takes an Option<T> and a transformation function, and returns an Option<U> with the transformed value if the input is Some, or None if the input is None.
steps.hint: The map function should check if the option is Some using the isSome type guard, apply the transformation function to the value, and return a new Some with the result. If the option is None, return None.
steps.expectedOutcome: A map function that transforms Option values when they exist, preserving the Option type.
successCriteria: The map function is defined with proper TypeScript generics, uses the isSome type guard, applies the transformation function to Some values, and returns the appropriate Option type.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your map function has the correct type signature (Option<T>, (value: T) => U) => Option<U>, uses the isSome type guard to check the input, and returns the appropriate Option type in both cases.
steps.feedbackWrong: The map function implementation needs work. Remember to create a function that takes an Option and a transformation function, checks if the Option is Some using isSome, applies the transformation to the value if it is, and returns None otherwise.

steps.title: Implement the getOrElse() helper
steps.instruction: Create a function named getOrElse that takes an Option<T> and a default value, and returns either the contained value or the default.
steps.hint: Write a function that checks if the option is Some using the isSome type guard, then returns the value if true, otherwise returns the default value.
steps.expectedOutcome: A getOrElse function that safely extracts values from Option with a fallback.
successCriteria: The getOrElse function is defined, uses the isSome type guard, and returns the correct value or default.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started getOrElse, but check the type guard usage and return types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The getOrElse function is missing or incorrect. Review the expected signature and logic.

steps.title: Test the Option helpers with example usage
steps.instruction: Create an example function named demonstrateOptionHelpers that uses some(), none(), map(), and getOrElse() to demonstrate the Option pattern in action.
steps.hint: Define a function that creates Option values, applies transformations with map(), and safely extracts values with getOrElse().
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a function that demonstrates practical usage of the Option helpers you built.
successCriteria: The demonstrateOptionHelpers function is defined and uses some(), none(), map(), and getOrElse() to show how the Option pattern works.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created the function, but it doesn't use all the required helpers (some, none, map, getOrElse). Make sure to include examples of each.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function is missing or doesn't properly demonstrate the Option helpers. Review how to use some(), none(), map(), and getOrElse().
